paras: The lynching threat against Olson at Bangor was a declaration by farmers near Bangor, Walworth County, Dakota Territory, in October 1888 that they would hang a farmer named Olson, who was accused of beating and kicking his wife until she lay in critical condition. Dispatches from Aberdeen on October 9 and 10 carried the threat to papers in Dakota, Illinois, Nebraska and Washington, D.C., some under headlines that approved of it. No English-language paper reported the outcome, but a Swedish-language weekly in St. Paul reported in late November that Olson had been lynched.

According to an Aberdeen dispatch dated October 9, the accused man farmed fourteen miles southwest of Bangor and had married a "Miss Bottles" some months earlier. The Washington Evening Star's version placed the farm fourteen miles west of Bangor and gave the bride's name as "Miss Battle"; neither account named the husband. A dispatch sent a day later identified him as "a farmer named Olson, living near Bangor."

A few days before the dispatches, he reportedly ordered his wife to go with him to the field to help with stacking, and she refused because she was sick and "in a delicate condition." He was accused of then nearly tearing off one of her ears, beating her with an ox goad and kicking her until she fainted before reaching the field. She was said to have lain in critical condition since.

The October 9 dispatch said that Bangor "anticipates a lynching bee to-night" and that the farmers had banded together to hang him that night. The October 10 dispatch credited the news to a courier who had come into Aberdeen from Bangor "yesterday afternoon" and reported that the farmers "declare they will hang the wretch."

The English-language reports, the last of them reprinted on November 8, did not say whether the farmers carried out the threat, whether Olson was arrested, or whether his wife recovered. On November 21 Skaffaren, a Swedish-language weekly in St. Paul, reported in its Dakota column that Olson, living near Bangor, had been arrested for cruel violence against "several women," had been threatened with lynching right after his arrest, and "has now actually been lynched." The item gave no date, place or manner of death, and no other paper found confirms it.

Headline writers treated the threat as a deserved punishment more than a crime. The Rock Island Argus headed the story "Lyneb [Lynch] Law Is Abominable, But—," and the Bismarck Weekly Tribune called it "Would Get His Just Deserts" and referred to the husband as "the brute." The Evening Star's "May Be Lynched for His Cruelty" and the Beatrice Daily Express's "Will Lynch a Wife-Beater" were plainer.

In Dakota the Mitchell Capital printed the October 11 version as "Will Hang the Wretch," with a subhead promising that a band of farmers would "Jerk a Wife Beater Into Eternity," and the Wahpeton Times reprinted the same item on November 8. Shorter versions ran in the Dickinson Press's "Week's News in Dakota" on October 13 and in the Webster Reporter and Farmer's crime digest "Man's Wicked Doings" on October 18. Every English version called Olson "the wretch" or "the brute," stated the beating as fact, and gave no account from him or his wife.

The two Aberdeen dispatches differed in where the farm lay and in the wife's maiden name, and the Olson text carried an October 10 dateline in the Argus and October 11 in the Mitchell Capital. The only report of a killing, Skaffaren's, appeared six weeks later and differed from the dispatches in saying that Olson had been arrested and that his violence was against several women, so the outcome rests on that single item.

A band of farmers acting without authority threatened to hang Olson to punish a beating (A1, A4); only Skaffaren, six weeks later and in a garbled version, says he was killed (A10), and no English-language report confirms it.
Every English report traces to Aberdeen dispatches relaying one courier from Bangor (A1, A4); the claim that Olson was lynched rests on a single Swedish-language item (A10).

accounts.gist: An unnamed farmer 14 miles from Bangor beat his sick wife with an ox goad and kicked her; Bangor 'anticipates a lynching bee to-night'.

accounts.label: Aberdeen dispatch of Oct. 10-11 (courier's report)
accounts.gist: A courier from Bangor said farmers had banded together and would hang Olson for beating and kicking his wife.

accounts.label: Skaffaren (Swedish-language, St. Paul)
accounts.gist: Olson was arrested for cruel violence against several women, threatened with lynching right after, and has now been lynched.

framing.detail: The Rock Island Argus headed it 'Lynch Law Is Abominable, But—', condemning lynching in principle while implying this case was an exception.
The Bismarck Weekly Tribune's headline 'Would Get His Just Deserts' and its 'the brute' endorsed the threatened hanging.
The Evening Star's 'May Be Lynched for His Cruelty' reported the threat without comment.
Dakota papers ran the Aberdeen text in digests and patent pages ('Will Hang the Wretch', 'Week's News in Dakota', 'Man's Wicked Doings'), calling Olson 'the wretch'.

conflicts.note: Detail differences between the Oct. 9 and Oct. 10 dispatches.
Likely a transmission variant; the Olson-naming dispatch gives none.
Skaffaren's late item is the only report of a killing; it also says Olson was arrested and that his violence was against 'several women', details that match no English report.
